news.title: Coding agents build robot training worlds while frontier models struggle on new tests
news.summary: Pranjal Aggarwal and Sean Welleck introduced Gym-Anything, a framework for creating robotics simulations with coding agents. In the RoboWorld suite, the strongest tested models completed no held-out tasks and averaged just 0.06 reward.
news.details: Constructing a realistic virtual training environment can require extensive expert labor before a robot starts learning. Pranjal Aggarwal and Sean Welleck propose Gym-Anything, where coding agents build simulations and an adversarial audit checks whether their physics and tasks satisfy explicit criteria. The selection of physical work draws on US economic activity instead of focusing solely on familiar toy demonstrations.
news.technical_novelty: RoboWorld contains 25 simulations, 175 training environments and 25 held-out test environments. According to the authors, even the strongest evaluated frontier models failed every test task, averaging 0.06 reward. Reward is a numerical simulator score, not a real-world robot success percentage. The paper also explores learning from repeated attempts, privileged teachers that can inspect simulator state, and demonstrations produced by code policies.
news.engineering_impact: The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Contact, friction and task conditions should be checked against real observations before relying on simulated scores.
news.limitations: Several approaches improved the measured results, but transfer to physical hardware remains unproven. Automatically generated worlds can misrepresent friction, contact dynamics and unexpected events in actual industrial settings.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint; experimental results are reported by the authors.
news.body:
Constructing a realistic virtual training environment can require extensive expert labor before a robot starts learning. Pranjal Aggarwal and Sean Welleck propose Gym-Anything, where coding agents build simulations and an adversarial audit checks whether their physics and tasks satisfy explicit criteria. The selection of physical work draws on US economic activity instead of focusing solely on familiar toy demonstrations.

RoboWorld contains 25 simulations, 175 training environments and 25 held-out test environments. According to the authors, even the strongest evaluated frontier models failed every test task, averaging 0.06 reward. Reward is a numerical simulator score, not a real-world robot success percentage. The paper also explores learning from repeated attempts, privileged teachers that can inspect simulator state, and demonstrations produced by code policies.

Several approaches improved the measured results, but transfer to physical hardware remains unproven. Automatically generated worlds can misrepresent friction, contact dynamics and unexpected events in actual industrial settings.

The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Contact, friction and task conditions should be checked against real observations before relying on simulated scores.

news.title: A robot map estimates how doors and drawers respond to force
news.summary: Dibyendu Ghosh proposed PhysVLMM, a scene map that represents uncertainty about the mechanics of moving parts. In tests involving doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identified joint types in 86% of held-out pulls.
news.details: A conventional room map can show a robot where a door is without revealing which way it moves or how much force opening it requires. Dibyendu Ghosh proposes PhysVLMM, a map that stores probabilistic beliefs about articulated components. After a measured pull, the system updates its estimate, and a planner can ask whether an action is likely to succeed within a stated risk limit.
news.technical_novelty: Watching a part move does not uniquely reveal its dynamics. Even a measured pull directly informs only the tested component and direction. The method therefore maintains a distribution of possible properties, shares relevant evidence with visually similar untested parts and can abstain when the evidence is inadequate.
news.engineering_impact: The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Force, motion direction and uncertainty should remain measurable. False-safe predictions and their consequences need separate testing.
news.limitations: In real doors and drawers across 18 homes, the method identified joint types in 86% of held-out pulls versus 48% for a single-view learned comparison. Its prediction error measured by CRPS was 0.323 versus 0.544 for differentiable simulation, while computation took 13 milliseconds versus 230 seconds per case. These are results for the studied objects, not a universal safety guarantee.

news.body:
A conventional room map can show a robot where a door is without revealing which way it moves or how much force opening it requires. Dibyendu Ghosh proposes PhysVLMM, a map that stores probabilistic beliefs about articulated components. After a measured pull, the system updates its estimate, and a planner can ask whether an action is likely to succeed within a stated risk limit.

Watching a part move does not uniquely reveal its dynamics. Even a measured pull directly informs only the tested component and direction. The method therefore maintains a distribution of possible properties, shares relevant evidence with visually similar untested parts and can abstain when the evidence is inadequate.

In real doors and drawers across 18 homes, the method identified joint types in 86% of held-out pulls versus 48% for a single-view learned comparison. Its prediction error measured by CRPS was 0.323 versus 0.544 for differentiable simulation, while computation took 13 milliseconds versus 230 seconds per case. These are results for the studied objects, not a universal safety guarantee.

The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Force, motion direction and uncertainty should remain measurable. False-safe predictions and their consequences need separate testing.

news.title: Human fingertip contact becomes training data for robot hands
news.summary: Haozhe Zhang and collaborators introduced TouchBridge, a method for converting human demonstrations into robot training data using tactile correspondence. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, the converted data yielded 72.5% average success versus 77.5% with directly teleoperated robot demonstrations.
news.details: Human fingers and robotic fingers have different geometry, so copying a hand trajectory does not guarantee the same contact with an object. Haozhe Zhang and collaborators propose TouchBridge, a combined hardware-and-software system with a wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robotic interface. Both capture visual and fingertip tactile information to establish correspondence across different hand designs.
news.technical_novelty: Its Tac-Retarget component aligns fingertip contact patches and their spatial relationships using measured touch. The authors report that this conversion does not require an object mesh, an object-pose estimate or a physics simulator. With visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, the transformed examples are used to fine-tune a pretrained model that maps visual observations and instructions to robot actions.
news.engineering_impact: The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Sevenfold faster collection does not remove the need to test contact on target objects. The 72.5% and 77.5% results matter alongside failure costs.
news.limitations: Across four physical contact-rich tasks, policies trained solely on converted human demonstrations reached 72.5% average success. An equal number of robot demonstrations collected through direct teleoperation yielded 77.5%, while human data collection was seven times faster. These results are promising for collecting examples efficiently, but cover specific tasks, hands and training conditions, not every object or robotic platform.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint; experimental results are reported by the authors.
news.body:
Human fingers and robotic fingers have different geometry, so copying a hand trajectory does not guarantee the same contact with an object. Haozhe Zhang and collaborators propose TouchBridge, a combined hardware-and-software system with a wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robotic interface. Both capture visual and fingertip tactile information to establish correspondence across different hand designs.

Its Tac-Retarget component aligns fingertip contact patches and their spatial relationships using measured touch. The authors report that this conversion does not require an object mesh, an object-pose estimate or a physics simulator. With visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, the transformed examples are used to fine-tune a pretrained model that maps visual observations and instructions to robot actions.

Across four physical contact-rich tasks, policies trained solely on converted human demonstrations reached 72.5% average success. An equal number of robot demonstrations collected through direct teleoperation yielded 77.5%, while human data collection was seven times faster. These results are promising for collecting examples efficiently, but cover specific tasks, hands and training conditions, not every object or robotic platform.

The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Sevenfold faster collection does not remove the need to test contact on target objects. The 72.5% and 77.5% results matter alongside failure costs.

news.title: Millions of labeled short actions expose the structure of long robot tasks
news.summary: Xueyuan Wei and collaborators introduced RoboAtom-Data, a dataset of 1.45 million robot trajectories with consistent time-aligned action labels. It covers 6.88 million skill segments and 16,882.1 recorded hours, with evaluations in skill recognition and robot control.
news.details: An instruction such as clearing a table hides many steps: approach, grasp, move and release. Yet large robot datasets often store only the overall task instruction. Xueyuan Wei and collaborators propose RoboAtom-Data, which assigns consistent time-aligned labels to short, or atomic, actions so learning systems can recover the structure of longer behavior.
news.technical_novelty: The authors describe annotations spanning 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments and 16,882.1 hours. Their pipeline combines human annotation, propagation of labels across repeated skill sequences and multiple quality-control stages. They also introduce RoboAtom-Bench to test both skill recognition and the localization of skill boundaries in time.
news.engineering_impact: The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Consistent time-aligned labels help combine datasets, but incorrect skill boundaries can distort later learning.
news.limitations: According to the paper, an annotation model trained on these labels outperformed the evaluated open and closed models on both RoboAtom-Bench and an external WGO-Bench. In control experiments, atomic-action supervision combined with hierarchical execution improved task success on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin. The abstract does not specify every numerical gain, and the promised release of data and tools is not equivalent to an already verified public download.

news.body:

Xueyuan Wei and collaborators propose RoboAtom-Data, which assigns consistent time-aligned labels to short, or atomic, actions so learning systems can recover the structure of longer behavior.

The authors describe annotations spanning 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments and 16,882.1 hours. Their pipeline combines human annotation, propagation of labels across repeated skill sequences and multiple quality-control stages. They also introduce RoboAtom-Bench to test both skill recognition and the localization of skill boundaries in time.

According to the paper, an annotation model trained on these labels outperformed the evaluated open and closed models on both RoboAtom-Bench and an external WGO-Bench. In control experiments, atomic-action supervision combined with hierarchical execution improved task success on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin. The abstract does not specify every numerical gain, and the promised release of data and tools is not equivalent to an already verified public download.

The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Consistent time-aligned labels help combine datasets, but incorrect skill boundaries can distort later learning.

news.title: One learning pipeline adapts coordinated manipulation to different robot hands
news.summary: Xiaoyu Yang and Nan Wu introduced AcrossDEX 1.0, a pipeline connecting human-motion pretraining with two-handed robot manipulation. In their experiments, direct regression reached 100% success on Inspire-hand object reorientation and 93.3% on Allegro-hand reorientation.
news.details: Robotic hands can have very different numbers of joints yet face similar problems: hold an object, turn it and coordinate both wrists and fingers. Xiaoyu Yang and Nan Wu propose AcrossDEX 1.0, a pipeline combining human-motion pretraining, simulation-based expert learning, robot demonstration collection and visual feedback during execution.
news.technical_novelty: During pretraining, the system predicts one second of bimanual motion from five images and thirty annotated hand states recorded over the preceding second. Shared wrist representations are retained when adapting to robots, while finger control accounts for the mechanics of each hand. The researchers tested six-channel Inspire hands and sixteen-joint Allegro hands, with control predictions revised from new camera observations.
news.engineering_impact: The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Shared wrist representations and hand-specific finger control support transfer studies. Results still depend on the object and control method.
news.limitations: In their evaluations, direct regression achieved 40.6% success on opening and returning a lid, 100% on Inspire object reorientation and 93.3% on Allegro reorientation. Flow matching achieved 90% on Allegro reorientation. These figures describe different tasks and conditions, not an overall ranking of robotic hands. Constraining new plans with previous plans can improve continuity.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint; experimental results are reported by the authors.
news.body:
Robotic hands can have very different numbers of joints yet face similar problems: hold an object, turn it and coordinate both wrists and fingers. Xiaoyu Yang and Nan Wu propose AcrossDEX 1.0, a pipeline combining human-motion pretraining, simulation-based expert learning, robot demonstration collection and visual feedback during execution.

During pretraining, the system predicts one second of bimanual motion from five images and thirty annotated hand states recorded over the preceding second. Shared wrist representations are retained when adapting to robots, while finger control accounts for the mechanics of each hand. The researchers tested six-channel Inspire hands and sixteen-joint Allegro hands, with control predictions revised from new camera observations.

In their evaluations, direct regression achieved 40.6% success on opening and returning a lid, 100% on Inspire object reorientation and 93.3% on Allegro reorientation. Flow matching achieved 90% on Allegro reorientation. These figures describe different tasks and conditions, not an overall ranking of robotic hands. Constraining new plans with previous plans can improve continuity.

The engineering value lies in reproducibility rather than a headline number alone. A replication needs the hardware configuration, training data, evaluation protocol, control frequency and stopping conditions. Comparisons should use consistent compute budgets and attempt counts. Rare failures deserve separate analysis rather than disappearing into an average. Until an independent team reproduces the result on another setup, an improvement is evidence within the authors' experimental conditions, not a universal property of the method. Shared wrist representations and hand-specific finger control support transfer studies. Results still depend on the object and control method.

technology_signal.title: Testable skills matter more than striking demonstrations
technology_signal.summary: New research emphasizes structured data, measurements and testable results.
technology_signal.implications: The next step is independent testing on different robots and real tasks.
